cim: The challenges of artificial intelligence in education shaped UNESCO’s participation in the 14th País Digital Summit
cim_eredeti: The challenges of artificial intelligence in education shaped UNESCO’s participation in the 14th País Digital Summit
szoveg_eredeti:
With more than 500 in-person participants and 1,900 views of the online livestream, LAC Digital Learning Week 2026 was held in Santiago on 6 and 7 October 2026, providing a regional continuation of the discussions held during Digital Learning Week in September at UNESCO Headquarters in Paris.

Co-organized by the UNESCO Regional Office in Santiago and Fundación País Digital, within the framework of the 14th País Digital Summit, the event brought key international reflections into dialogue with the educational realities, needs and priorities of Latin America and the Caribbean.

The sessions addressed the need to advance towards an inclusive, ethical and human-centred digital transformation, with particular emphasis on the pedagogical use of artificial intelligence, strengthening teachers’ capacities and regional cooperation.

“At UNESCO, we believe that artificial intelligence can offer extraordinary opportunities to expand access to learning, strengthen teachers and students, and support the management of education systems. But we also believe that no technology can replace what lies at the heart of education: human interaction, critical thinking, creativity, empathy and the collective construction of knowledge,” said Esther Kuisch Laroche, Director of the UNESCO Regional Office in Santiago.

The event began with a plenary session in which Catalina Araya (Fundación País Digital) and Valtencir Mendes (UNESCO Santiago) presented the main discussions from Digital Learning Week in Paris. Mendes also shared progress on the Observatory on Artificial Intelligence in Education for Latin America and the Caribbean. From a humanistic perspective, Cristián del Campo (Universidad Alberto Hurtado) and Ignacio Sánchez (Fundación Encuentros del Futuro) reflected on the human dimension of technological transformation. Macarena Álvarez, Moana Tepano and Annais Molina shared experiences of youth leadership and innovation, while Roberto Porzecanski (Fundación Ceibal) addressed progress in educational transformation across the region.

The panel “PISA speaks to us: what role should technology play in education?”, moderated by Amparo Naranjo (UNESCO Santiago), featured Magdalena Plant (Ministry of Education of Chile) and Ignacio Cáceres (SLEP Santa Corina). The discussion examined the challenges highlighted by PISA results and the role of technology and artificial intelligence in improving learning, emphasizing the importance of strengthening foundational skills, critical thinking, teacher education and digital citizenship. Finally, Pablo Christiny (Fundación Nativo Digital) presented the Digital Well-being Barometer, providing evidence on the digital habits of children and adolescents. The session highlighted the importance of integrating technology into education in pedagogically sound, critical and evidence-based ways.

The second day continued with specialized dialogue sessions addressing some of the main opportunities and tensions surrounding the use of AI in education in Latin America and the Caribbean.

The session “TVET governance in the age of AI: needs and strategies for Latin America and the Caribbean” brought together UNESCO specialists and representatives of technical and vocational education and training institutions to discuss governance and adaptation challenges in the face of technological and labour-market transformations. Ramón Iriarte (UNESCO Paris) highlighted the role of Centres of Excellence as spaces for innovation and collaboration, while Amparo Naranjo (UNESCO Santiago) and Alejandra Ortiz (UNESCO Mexico) presented progress on the regional model and its pilot implementation in Mexico. Francisco Norberto Varela Cruz (CONALEP) and Elliot Gama Ramírez (DGETI) shared experiences of strengthening links between technical education and the productive sector. Finally, Soledad Patiño Villalba (UNESCO Paris) presented the Global Skills Academy initiative, aimed at strengthening digital skills for the future of work.

In this context, a closed meeting of focal points of the Regional Alliance for Educational Transformation and Innovation (ARTIE) was held, with representatives from 15 countries in Latin America and the Caribbean. The meeting provided an opportunity to share progress within the network, exchange experiences and strengthen regional coordination to promote joint educational transformation and innovation initiatives.

The session “New frontiers for teaching practice: teaching and learning with AI” brought together Darío Riquelme (University of Chile), Alejandra Meza (Red EdTech) and Pablo Donoso (Matific), who explored the opportunities and challenges of integrating artificial intelligence into teaching and learning processes. Riquelme highlighted the importance of strengthening institutional governance and reviewing assessment strategies; Meza shared experiences of using AI to foster students’ creativity and experimentation; and Donoso examined its potential to develop mathematical reasoning, critical thinking and personalized learning. The discussion emphasized the fundamental role of teachers and the pedagogical decisions that guide the use of these technologies.

Finally, the programme on 7 October concluded with the round table “From data to decision-making: AI in curriculum management”, which brought together Nicole Faure and Jaime Balladares (researchers from the FONIDE project) and Karla Cantuarias (Fundación Kodea). Faure and Balladares presented preliminary findings on the use of AI in teaching practice, highlighting opportunities to reduce administrative workload, improve planning and personalize learning, as well as challenges related to access gaps, professional autonomy, and ethical and pedagogical guidance. Cantuarias, for her part, shared progress on “Future Teachers in AI”, an initiative aimed at incorporating artificial intelligence competencies into initial teacher education through collaboration with universities.

This article is related to the United Nation’s Sustainable Development Goals.
